headline: 5th Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan Awards conferred on Best Performing Cities and Wards on Swachh Vayu Diwas 2026; Compendium of Best Management Practices under NCAP released
fullText:
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change

5th Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan Awards conferred on Best Performing Cities and Wards on Swachh Vayu Diwas 2026; Compendium of Best Management Practices under NCAP released

Local Bodies must engage in All-inclusive and Whole of Society Approach to address the issue of Air Pollution: Chairperson (NGT)

Fighting Air Pollution a Continuous Programme, requiring Citizen-led Movement in Mission Mode: Secretary (EFCC)

07 SEP 2026 2:29PM by PIB Delhi

The Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) organized the Swachh Vayu Diwas 2026 today, on the International Day of Clean Air for Blue Skies. The event was presided over by Chairperson, National Green Tribunal (NGT), Justice Prakash Shrivastava as Chief Guest. Other dignitaries gracing the occasion included Secretary (EFCC), Shri Tanmay Kumar; Chairperson (CAQM), Shri Rajesh Verma; DG (Forest) and Special Secretary (EFCC), Shri Sushil Kumar Awasthi; Chairperson (CPCB), Shri Amandeep Garg; and AS (EFCC), Shri Ashutosh Agnihotri. Officials from Union Ministries, Multilateral organisations, Mayors, District Collectors and Municipal Commissioners of award-winning Cities and wards, besides officials from MoEFCC, CPCB and CAQM were present.

In his address, Justice Shrivastava appreciated the efforts of Union and State Governments under the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP). He stated that this is an occasion to recognise efforts made by cities/wards across the country to ensure the quality of air is maintained within the prescribed parameters. “The awardees have shown that clean air is not an aspiration but a practical goal that can be achieved with proper planning and ground level implementation”, he noted. The Chairperson highlighted that clean air is a fundamental need rather than a luxury. He stated, “Development and Environmental conservation are not at cross purposes but can go together while maintaining the quality of life for the citizens. It is the responsibility of each citizen to ensure that generations to come are able to live in a clean environment”.

Justice Shrivastava called air pollution a complex challenge as it doesn't know political boundaries and a multitude of sources contribute to it. The Chairperson stressed that the frontline institutions are the urban/rural local bodies that ensure the effective implementation of the National vision. With the Swachh Sarvekshan Awards, the Government recognises the efforts of all stakeholders in the field of air quality management, who put in efforts to ensure that the air quality remains within the prescribed limits, he stated. “It is essential that local bodies strive for prevention of pollution generation at source by making citizens aware; adopt latest technologies to tackle the issue; and engage in an all-inclusive and whole of society approach to address the issue”, he added.

In his address on the occasion, Secretary (EFCC), Shri Tanmay Kumar informed that the Government of India is taking a multi-pronged, coordinated and scientific approach towards tackling air pollution as per Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi's vision. Public representatives are being incorporated in this mission to encourage participation of citizens to fight air pollution as well ensure capacity building of all stakeholders.

Shri Kumar talked about the NCAP that provides a framework where cities have their own strategies to ensure clean air, while the PRANA portal tracks various parameters of air quality management for 130 cities under NCAP. He said that fighting air pollution is a continuous programme, not a one-off activity. It requires a citizen-led movement in mission mode to achieve a clean environment for generations to come. He congratulated all the awardees for their efforts and encouraged them to make air quality management a jan-bhagidari movement.

Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan Awards

On this occasion, MoEFCC awarded the best performing Cities and Wards under National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), ranked as part of the 5th Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan. Swachh Vayu Survekshan Framework released in 2022-23 on measures taken by cities on road dust, SWM, vehicular emissions, industrial pollution, C&D waste management, other emissions (DG sets and commercial establishments), IEC activities.

The awards were based on participation and ranking of all 130 cities in 3 groups (Population below 3 Lakh; 3-10 Lakh; & above 10 Lakh), through the process involving self-assessment by cities, approval by State-level Monitoring Committee, evaluation by CPCB, field verification by Independent Committees and selection of 10 best performing cities.

List of Swachh Vayu Sarvekshan Awardees

Achievements under National Clean Air Programme (NCAP)

During Swachh Vayu Diwas, progress and achievements made under the NCAP, a flagship initiative launched to improve air quality across 130 cities in 24 States/UTs, were highlighted. A performance linked grant of ₹ 16,425 crore has been provided to 130 NCAP cities as critical gap funding to implement air pollution mitigation measures.

NCAP has shown positive results in terms of achieving reduction in PM10 levels in 2025-26 with respect to the levels of FY 2017-18:

108 out of 130 cities have shown improvement in PM10 levels.

72 cities have achieved reduction in PM10 concentrations of more than 20%.

26 cities have recorded reductions exceeding 40%.

14 cities have met National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS)

Compendium of Best Management Practices under NCAP

During the event, the Compendium of Best Management Practices under NCAP was released. It highlights best practices and successful air quality improvement measures implemented by cities and State Pollution Control Boards/Committees under NCAP, in various sectors namely, Road dust control, Vehicular pollution, industrial pollution, Solid and Construction & Demolition (C&D) waste management, Control of open burning, Greening, Use of technology and Public Outreach. These best practices would be helpful in replicating them by other cities and SPCBs.

headline: Government Strengthens Transparency and Timely Delivery of Scholarships for Scheduled Caste Students
fullText:
Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment

Government Strengthens Transparency and Timely Delivery of Scholarships for Scheduled Caste Students

DBT and Aadhaar-Seeded Bank Accounts Enable Direct Transfer of the Central Share to Eligible Students

Web-Based Monitoring, Periodic Reviews and Field Visits Reinforce Accountability across States and Union Territories

07 SEP 2026 2:22PM by PIB Delhi

The Central Government has strengthened the delivery, monitoring and accountability framework for the Centrally Sponsored Schemes of Post-Matric Scholarships for Scheduled Castes and Pre-Matric Scholarships for Scheduled Castes and Others. The schemes support eligible students of recognised institutions across the country and are implemented through State Governments and Union Territory Administrations.

The scholarship programmes are open-ended and demand-driven. The Post-Matric Scholarship Scheme has been implemented through Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) from 2021-22, while the Pre-Matric Scholarship Scheme has followed the DBT mode from 2022-23. Under this system, the Central share is released directly into the Aadhaar-seeded bank accounts of eligible applicants.

Release of the Central share is linked to the transmission by States and Union Territories of data relating to payment of their respective share on the National Scholarship Portal. This digital process enables Centre- and State-level monitoring of scholarship applications and disbursement, promotes timely delivery and reduces the scope for diversion or misuse of funds.

Complaints or representations concerning implementation are promptly forwarded to the concerned State Government or Union Territory Administration, which is the implementing agency, for examination and remedial action under the applicable procedure. The concerned authorities take appropriate administrative action wherever required.

The reformed framework places emphasis on comprehensive accountability, continuous monitoring and transparency. Implementation is reviewed periodically through meetings at the National, Regional and State levels, as well as through field visits. National conferences and Chintan Shivirs are also organised to assess scheme performance, with the participation of Union and State Ministers, senior officers and other officials from the Centre and the States.

Together, DBT, Aadhaar seeding, portal-based data exchange and regular reviews create a traceable delivery chain from sanction to receipt. The measures are intended to ensure that scholarship assistance reaches eligible students directly and supports their continued education without avoidable delays.

The Ministry of Social Justice And Empowerment remains committed to strengthening educational access for students from disadvantaged communities through transparent, technology-enabled and accountable scholarship delivery systems.

For more information, visit: https://socialjustice.gov.in/schemes/23

headline: Luxembourg Minister of Economy, SME, Energy & Tourism Mr Lex Delles calls on Union Minister Dr Jitendra Singh, proposes identifying concrete areas of collaboration, primarily in the Space sector
fullText:
Ministry of Science & Technology

Luxembourg Minister of Economy, SME, Energy & Tourism Mr Lex Delles calls on Union Minister Dr Jitendra Singh, proposes identifying concrete areas of collaboration, primarily in the Space sector

Dr Jitendra Singh says, India-Luxembourg relations provide a favourable basis for taking cooperation into newer areas, refers to virtual meeting which PM Shri Narendra Modi had with his Luxembourg counterpart in 2020

India and Luxembourg explore new opportunities in AI, quantum technologies, life sciences and commercial space

Dr Jitendra Singh calls for structured engagement between Indian and Luxembourg institutions, research ecosystems and industry

Existing space partnership provides strong foundation for wider India-Luxembourg cooperation in emerging technologies

07 SEP 2026 2:15PM by PIB Delhi

Lex Delles, Minister of the Economy, SME, Energy and Tourism, Govt of Luxembourg, currently on India visit, today called on Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science & Technology and Earth Sciences and Minister of State for the Department of Space, Dr. Jitendra Singh, and proposed identifying concrete areas of collaboration between the two countries, primarily in the Space sector, as also in other emerging technologies and life sciences.

The proposed mechanism could also explore cooperation in areas including Artificial Intelligence, quantum technologies, advanced materials and life sciences, and help develop specific inputs from both sides ahead of the proposed State Visit of Luxembourg to India in January 2027.

The bilateral meeting between the two Ministers discussed the current status of India-Luxembourg cooperation in Space, future developments in the sector, opportunities for further institutional and commercial collaboration, and preparations for the proposed State Visit.

The Luxembourg delegation included senior officials from the Minister’s Cabinet, economic policy, industry, new technologies and research, as well as the Luxembourg Space Agency. The Indian side included senior officials from the Department of Science & Technology, Department of Space and Ministry of External Affairs.

Dr. Jitendra Singh said that the warmth and strong foundation of India-Luxembourg relations provide a favourable basis for taking cooperation into newer and deeper areas. He also referred to the virtual meeting which PM Sh Narendra Modi had with his Luxembourg counterpart in 2020.

Dr Jitendra Singh also referred to the considerable common ground between the two countries in science technology and innovation and said that the strengths of both sides could be brought together in emerging areas with high potential for mutual benefit.

The Minister said that Space remains an important pillar of the bilateral partnership, with India and Luxembourg already having an MoU on cooperation in the exploration and use of outer space for peaceful purposes, signed in February 2022. The partnership has also developed a commercial dimension, including communication satellite transponder leasing and the launch of two Luxembourg satellites on commercial terms onboard PSLV. IN-SPACe and the Luxembourg Space Agency have also been engaging to promote greater interaction between the two countries’ space ecosystems.

Dr. Jitendra Singh shared India’s broader space roadmap, including the importance of navigation and communication satellites in the near term and the country’s long-term ambition of establishing an Indian space station by 2035 and undertaking a human landing on the Moon by 2040. He said the expanding participation of the private sector in India’s space programme is also opening up new possibilities for international and commercial partnerships.

The two sides discussed opportunities for greater engagement of Luxembourg’s space industry with India’s rapidly expanding private space ecosystem. Potential areas identified from the Indian side include Earth Observation imagery, communication transponders, commercial satellite and satellite-subsystem realisation, launch vehicle services, ground stations and mission support. Luxembourg-based companies, including SES, are already engaged with Indian entities and IN-SPACe on opportunities relating to satellite capacity, user terminals and satellite and ground subsystems.

Artificial Intelligence and high-performance computing emerged as another important area of potential cooperation. Dr. Jitendra Singh spoke about India’s efforts to expand computing capacity, procure additional GPUs and develop indigenous large language models suited to the country’s linguistic diversity. The Luxembourg side shared its plans for a new AI-oriented high-performance computing facility and expressed interest in enabling greater interaction with the private sector. The two sides discussed the possibility of connecting Indian and Luxembourg companies and institutions in this area.

Quantum technologies were also discussed as an area offering significant scope for collaboration. Dr. Jitendra Singh spoke about India’s National Quantum Mission and the progress made in quantum communication, computing, sensing and related areas. He said quantum technologies have applications across sectors, including healthcare, security and space, and that optical communication in conjunction with the space sector could provide a particularly promising area for cooperation between India and Luxembourg.

In life sciences and biotechnology, Dr. Jitendra Singh spoke about India’s BioE3 policy and the country’s focus on biotechnology-led economic and scientific development. He referred to the potential for collaboration with Luxembourg institutions such as the Luxembourg Institute of Health and the Luxembourg Centre for Systems Biomedicine, particularly in areas of common interest including neurodegenerative diseases and Alzheimer’s disease.

The Minister also spoke about India’s growing public-private approach to vaccine development and medical research and the recent opening up of nuclear medicine research to the private sector. He said the development could create further opportunities for international institutions and industry to participate in areas of universal health relevance.

Minister Lex Delles spoke about Luxembourg’s growing engagement with India in space, satellite communications, Artificial Intelligence, cybersecurity and high-performance computing, and the opportunities for Luxembourg companies to deepen their activities in India. He also spoke about the importance of greater interaction between the two countries’ government institutions and private-sector ecosystems.

The meeting also discussed the proposed State Visit from Luxembourg to India in January 2027 as an opportunity to give greater momentum to bilateral cooperation. Dr. Jitendra Singh suggested that the Embassy could remain engaged with the concerned Indian institutions so that areas of interest are identified in advance and specific proposals can be developed for discussion during the visit.

The meeting reflected the growing breadth of India-Luxembourg cooperation from an established space partnership towards a wider engagement in AI, quantum technologies, life sciences, advanced technologies and commercial opportunities, with both sides exploring practical avenues to connect their respective institutions, research ecosystems and industries.

headline: Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Shri Piyush Goyal Calls for Trained Caregivers and Wider Hospital Participation in Heal in India Gateway
fullText:
Ministry of Commerce & Industry

Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Shri Piyush Goyal Calls for Trained Caregivers and Wider Hospital Participation in Heal in India Gateway

Shri Goyal Underscores the Importance of Seamless Patient Journeys, Global Promotion of Indian Healthcare and Quality-Focused Expansion Across States

India Should Target 10 Million Medical Value Tourists Annually: Shri Goyal

India’s Clinical Excellence, Advanced Technologies and 60–80% Lower Healthcare Costs Offer Huge Potential to Serve the World

Shri Goyal Stresses Quality, Professional Integrity and Zero Tolerance for Corruption in Healthcare Certification

07 SEP 2026 2:12PM by PIB Delhi

Union Minister of Commerce and Industry Shri Piyush Goyal today outlined a five-point action plan to strengthen India’s medical value tourism ecosystem and position the country as a gateway for international health and wellness services with the highest quality standards. Addressing the inaugural ceremony of Sanjeevani 2026 at Bharat Health Global Expo 2026 in New Delhi, Shri Goyal said the first priority should be to train and certify caregivers and develop a skilled workforce capable of providing healthcare of international standards.

The second point, he said, should be to encourage more hospitals to join the Heal in India gateway and publish honest and transparent treatment packages. He stressed that hospitals must follow ethical practices and never attempt to cheat patients, as one wrong action can lead to loss of goodwill, business and credibility for India.

As the third point, Shri Goyal called upon insurers and health-tech companies to build products and platforms that make the patient journey more seamless, ensuring timely reimbursements and greater availability of cashless payments. He also suggested that teleconsultations and telemedicine could be incorporated in a big way as an initial part of the medical value tourism journey.

The fourth point was the need to organise exhibitions and presentations across the world, establish facilitators and tie-ups with hospitals globally, and ensure that only National Accreditation Board for Hospitals & Healthcare Providers (NABH)-enabled, verified and panelled hospitals are allowed to treat patients coming from abroad. He stressed that NABH must maintain the highest standards with zero compromise.

As the fifth point, the Minister urged States to focus on quality in hospitals and wellness centres, expand their networks, make good-quality facilities globally visible and market these facilities for the welfare of patients. He called for medical value tourism to expand beyond metropolitan cities to Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities, creating jobs, opportunities and infrastructure while also helping upgrade healthcare for Indian patients.

Shri Goyal also suggested creating a pool of interpreters for patients arriving from different countries and speaking different languages, so that they have greater confidence and communication between patients and the medical system becomes easier.

The Minister emphasised that quality healthcare cannot be different for Indians and foreigners. He said India must ensure that every Indian patient receives the same high-quality healthcare as anyone coming from across the world. He said the country must give to its brothers and sisters what it would wish to receive itself and provide the same quality of healthcare to every person from India or abroad, without discrimination between rich and poor.

Shri Goyal stressed that those who entrust their lives to India by coming here for treatment must be treated with the highest care, concern and compassion. He said patients travelling abroad for healthcare, whether from Africa, Asia, America or Europe, experience anxiety as they enter a new country and seek clarity, dignity, ethical best practices and high integrity. They place their trust in India at every stage of their healthcare journey.

Highlighting the potential of India’s medical value tourism sector, Shri Goyal said India has clinical excellence, advanced technologies and healthcare costs 60-80 per cent lower than in other parts of the world, particularly the developed world. He said India also has compassion in abundance and appreciated the care and concern demonstrated by medical professionals across the country, from small nursing homes and doctors’ clinics to large municipal, private and government hospitals, often while working under considerable constraints.

The Minister said India’s pharmaceutical industry, medtech sector, diagnostics, traditional medicines including Ayurveda, Yoga and Unani, doctors, technicians, nurses, caregivers and hospitals collectively constitute the country’s strength and can make medical value tourism a potent instrument for serving the world. He said the sector has the potential to take India to the world, earn goodwill and serve people globally while creating a huge number of jobs and business opportunities in the manufacture of drugs, medical equipment and consumables, delivery of these products, hospital infrastructure and employment for doctors, teachers, nurses, technicians and other professionals.

Shri Goyal said that while 3.5 million patients have benefited from India’s medical value tourism ecosystem in the last seven years, the country’s target should be 10 million patients a year. He said India has the ability, capability, right doctors and the right ecosystem to achieve this. He emphasised that high standards, ethics, integrity and honesty must be maintained and urged healthcare providers to go the extra mile in caring for international patients.

Referring to the changing global healthcare landscape, Shri Goyal said the world is ageing while India is young and that many new-age diseases are spreading across the world. Healthcare costs are increasing and many parts of the world face long waiting lists even for doctors’, dentists’ and radiologists’ appointments, along with shortages of tertiary care. He said countries with which India is engaging through FTAs and business discussions want high-quality pharmaceuticals, doctors, technicians, nurses and caregivers from India in large numbers.

The Minister underlined the importance of preventive healthcare and the wellness ecosystem, referring to Ayurveda in Kerala and its spread across the country, wellness centres in the hills, and the care provided by nurses and young men and women working in the healthcare system. He said India is the land which can serve best and urged stakeholders not to miss the opportunity presented by the medical value tourism sector.

Emphasising collaboration, Shri Goyal said the purpose of Bharat Health was to bring the entire fragmented healthcare sector together and called upon stakeholders to work as collaborators and in cooperation with each other as a team. Shri Goyal said the healthcare sector is a perfect example of the need for collaboration and cooperation, as even a small error can have serious consequences.

He said India must maintain high-quality benchmarks and make quality visible to patients. He called for the scaling up of medical value tourism while maintaining high standards and said India should become the gateway for international health and wellness services with the highest quality standards available anywhere in the world.

Shri Goyal said the world is looking to India for high-quality pharmaceuticals, doctors, technicians, nurses and caregivers, and that India has the potential to respond to this demand. He reiterated that the sector presents an opportunity to serve the world while creating economic opportunities and societal benefits.

On healthcare for Indians, Shri Goyal highlighted Ayushman Bharat, under which poor people and their families do not have to worry about healthcare expenses when someone falls sick, as the government pays for their healthcare. He also highlighted the provision for all persons above 70 years of age, irrespective of income, to receive an additional healthcare cover of ₹5 lakh.

Shri Goyal said India’s approach to healthcare has always been guided by the principle of serving the world. Referring to the Upanishadic expression “Sarvesantu Niramaya”, meaning “may all beings be free from illness”, he said India has never viewed healthcare only within the boundaries of the country and has for thousands of years regarded healthcare as a shared responsibility of the entire world. He described “One World, One Health” as part of this basic ethos.

Recalling India’s response during the COVID period, Shri Goyal said India provided vaccines free of charge to countries that could not afford them and supplied vaccines to others at very low cost. While vaccines from the developed world were sold for around 25-30 dollars, Indian vaccines were available at around 2-3 dollars a dose. Shri Goyal stressed that India never profiteered at the cost of somebody else’s misery.

The Minister recalled that when medicines required during COVID were available in India, Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi decided to impose export restrictions on medicines being used at that time. He said that although very few medicines were proven for the treatment of COVID, paracetamol, certain other medicines, injections, injectables and consumables were required. He explained that export controls were introduced to safeguard India’s stock of medicines from being purchased or cornered by unscrupulous traders, certain companies or rich nations. Otherwise, only the rich could have received treatment while poorer and less-privileged populations, developing countries and India’s poor and lower-middle-class population could have been deprived of these medicines.

Shri Goyal said India not only ensured that everyone in the country who needed medicines received them, but also ensured equitable distribution of available medicines and equipment to countries across the world, whether rich or poor. More than 100 countries received medicines free of charge. He stressed that India did not profiteer from what it had and shared resources with others either free of charge or at cost.

Calling this the ethos of India, Shri Goyal said the third edition of Sanjeevani is bringing to the fore the potential contribution India can make to serve the country and the world. He said India must continue to ensure that healthcare for its own people is not compromised and referred to the various ways in which quality and timely healthcare are being made available.

The Minister also emphasised the importance of quality, ethics and integrity in the healthcare ecosystem. He said quality will determine the future of India and described the Quality Council of India as one of the most important organisations if India is to become a developed nation by 2047. He said maintaining high standards would be central to India’s future.

Shri Goyal stressed the importance of professional integrity in certification and said that the NABH system should be professionally run and free from influence. He stated that the Ministry or Government has not referred a single case and that the system is professionally managed. He urged stakeholders to complain if NABH or any certifying body engages in unethical practices and to approach the Ministry if such issues arise. He said the single largest focus of the Government is to eliminate corruption.

Shri Goyal concluded by reiterating that India must provide the same high-quality healthcare to every Indian patient as it provides to anyone coming from across the world. He said that just as every person wants the best healthcare for themselves and their families, it is the duty of the healthcare ecosystem to provide the same quality of healthcare to every single brother and sister from India or abroad, without discrimination between rich and poor.

headline: From an Aspirational District to Academic Excellence: How NFSC Support Empowered Dr. Abinash Mandal
fullText:
Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment

From an Aspirational District to Academic Excellence: How NFSC Support Empowered Dr. Abinash Mandal

07 SEP 2026 1:08PM by PIB Delhi

For scholars from socially and economically disadvantaged communities, pursuing advanced education can be difficult when financial limitations and geographical disadvantages restrict access to academic opportunities. Timely fellowship support can provide the stability needed to continue research and build a meaningful career in academia.

Demonstrating the impact of the National Fellowship for Scheduled Caste Students (NFSC) Scheme, Dr. Abinash Mandal, a 33-year-old scholar from Udalguri, Assam, overcame socio-economic and geographical barriers to earn his Ph.D. from Pondicherry University.

Hailing from an aspirational district, Dr. Mandal faced considerable financial constraints and limited access to advanced academic opportunities. The geographical disadvantages associated with living in a remote and underdeveloped district further restricted his access to quality educational resources, research exposure and opportunities for higher studies.

Belonging to a socially and economically disadvantaged community, he also encountered social barriers linked to his marginalised background. Together, these challenges made the pursuit of doctoral research particularly demanding. Nevertheless, his determination, perseverance and commitment to education enabled him to continue striving for academic excellence.

Dr. Mandal aspired to attain the highest level of academic qualification and contribute meaningfully to the fields of commerce and forensic accounting. His long-term goal was to engage in teaching, research and knowledge creation while inspiring students from deprived communities to pursue higher education and academic careers.

The encouragement of his family, combined with the opportunities provided by educational institutions, gave him the confidence to persevere. A decisive turning point came when he received assistance under the NFSC Scheme for the period from 2020 to 2024.

The Scheme provided him with a monthly fellowship of Rs 37,000 as a Junior Research Fellow (JRF), which was subsequently enhanced to Rs 42,000 per month following his progression to Senior Research Fellow (SRF). This sustained assistance enabled him to undertake full-time doctoral research without the burden of financial hardship.

The fellowship reduced his dependence on family resources and enabled him to access quality research materials, participate in academic conferences and pursue scholarly publication opportunities. The resulting financial stability allowed him to remain focused on his research and academic requirements.

With support under the Scheme, Dr. Mandal successfully progressed from JRF to SRF and completed his Ph.D. His research capabilities were strengthened during this period, resulting in publications in reputed international journals and presentations at prestigious institutions, including IIM Bodh Gaya, IIM Indore and IIT Delhi.

The fellowship also improved his economic well-being during his doctoral studies and opened better career opportunities upon completion of his Ph.D. It provided the foundation required for him to move from a financially constrained academic journey to a professional role in higher education.

Today, Dr. Mandal serves as Guest Faculty in the Department of Commerce at Pondicherry University, where he actively contributes to teaching, research and academic development. He continues to pursue his goal of advancing knowledge in commerce and forensic accounting while encouraging students from disadvantaged backgrounds to aim higher.

Dr. Abinash Mandal’s journey reflects the transformative role of the NFSC Scheme in enabling scholars from Scheduled Caste communities to overcome socio-economic barriers, achieve academic excellence and contribute meaningfully to academia and society.

headline: From Traditional skills to Rural Enterprises: How KVIC is creating new Livelihoods

Ministry of Micro,Small & Medium Enterprises

From Traditional skills to Rural Enterprises: How KVIC is creating new Livelihoods

From Struggles to Success: KVIC is Inspiring Entrepreneurial Journeys

07 SEP 2026 12:13PM by PIB Delhi

Across rural India, traditional skills and locally available resources are increasingly becoming the foundation for new entrepreneurial opportunities. From scientific beekeeping and value-added honey products to vetiver-based enterprises and banana-fibre products, rural entrepreneurs are demonstrating how local knowledge can be transformed into viable businesses and livelihood opportunities.

The Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC), under the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME), is supporting this transformation through training, financial assistance, improved tools and technology, market support and other interventions. Through initiatives such as the Khadi Vikas Yojana (KVY), Gramodyog Vikas Yojana (GVY) and the Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP), traditional skills are being strengthened with modern enterprise capabilities, enabling artisans and rural entrepreneurs to create sustainable livelihoods.

From Struggles to Success: Inspiring Entrepreneurial Journeys:

1. Shri T. Ajin: From Beekeeping to Building Livelihoods

In Kanyakumari, Tamil Nadu, Shri T. Ajin has turned his knowledge of beekeeping into a successful honey enterprise through his unit, Marthandam Honey Products. The enterprise produces AGMARK-certified honey and honey blended with dry fruits, adding value to traditional beekeeping.

But Shri Ajin’s contribution goes beyond his own enterprise. He trains farmers, particularly those from economically weaker sections and SC/ST communities, in modern beekeeping practices. He has also participated in State, Regional and District-level programmes, besides sharing his knowledge through All India Radio and Doordarshan.

His journey shows that how an entrepreneur can create impact through a successful business, and also by helping others in the community to find their own livelihood opportunities.

Shri B. Sundaraj: Turning Vetiver into an Enterprise

For Shri B. Sundaraj, a naturally fragrant plant became the foundation for a new business opportunity. Through his Pure Health Herbal Agarbathi Unit, he produces Agarbathi, herbal products, Vetiver Agarbathi and Vetiver Samburani.

With support under the Gramodyog Vikas Yojana (GVY) during 2024–25, Shri Sundaraj strengthened his manufacturing capabilities and expanded his product range. His story is an example of how local resources, traditional knowledge and a business idea can come together to create a sustainable village enterprise.

3. Shri M. Murugesan: Giving Agricultural Waste a New Life

Shri M. Murugesan has built an enterprise around this idea through his Banana Fibre Fancy Articles Making Unit under PMEGP. Through Om Banana Craft Private Limited, he converts banana fibre into attractive and useful fancy articles, showing how agricultural resources can be transformed into value-added products.

His work has also earned him Central and State Government awards. He regularly participates in exhibitions and awareness programmes and shares his knowledge through All India Radio, Doordarshan and training programmes. His journey demonstrates that rural enterprises can create value through new product development while making better use of local and natural resources.

Honey Mission: Turning Beekeeping into a Livelihood

One of the prominent initiatives in this journey is the Honey Mission, launched in 2017 to promote scientific beekeeping and create livelihood opportunities for farmers, tribal communities and unemployed youth. Under the programme, beneficiaries receive training along with bee boxes, live bee colonies and related toolkits. This enables them to take up beekeeping and gradually build it into a source of income.

The scale of the initiative can be seen in the numbers. According to the KVIC, around 2,46,000 bee boxes and bee colonies were distributed across the country between 2017–18 and 2025–26, which resulted in around 5,500 metric tonnes of honey production during 2025–26.

Beekeeping creates opportunities beyond honey production. Bees play an important role in pollination, creating a natural link between beekeeping, agriculture and biodiversity. Indian honey bees are cultivated by beekeepers across several States, including Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Odisha and the North-Eastern States, with livelihoods dependent on the activity.

Beekeeping can therefore serve not merely as a source of supplementary income, but as an entry point into a broader rural enterprise ecosystem.

From Tradition to Enterprise

The experiences of Shri T. Ajin, Shri B. Sundaraj and Shri M. Murugesan illustrate a larger opportunity for rural India: traditional skills and local resources can become the starting point for modern enterprises when supported by training, technology, finance, market access and entrepreneurship.

Through its network of programmes and interventions, KVIC continues to support this transition—helping rural communities preserve their traditional strengths while creating new economic opportunities around them.

From tradition to enterprise, from local resources to value-added products, and from individual skills to wider livelihoods, India’s village industries are becoming an important part of the country’s rural entrepreneurship story.
